wine.name: Ried Ulm Nussberg Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC
wine.classification: Erste Lage of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter, marked 1ÖTW on the label
wine.grapes: A field blend of nine white varieties planted together, by the house's sheet: Weissburgunder, Neuburger, Welschriesling, Grüner Veltliner, Silvaner, Zierfandler, Rotgipfler, Traminer and Riesling.
wine.sites: Ried Ulm, a very steep south facing slope at the eastern end of the Nussberg above the Danube, on calcareous shell limestone, a former coral reef by the house's account; biodynamic since 2008, certified from the 2011 harvest.
wine.making: The nine varieties are picked, pressed and fermented together, as the DAC requires, once any grapes touched by botrytis are sorted out. About three quarters of the must ferments in cooled stainless steel and the rest in large old oak casks; the lots rest about ten months on their fine lees before they are brought together and bottled.
wine.glass: Ripe pear, quince and yellow apple with white pepper and a touch of honeysuckle over a salty, chalky edge; broad yet fresh, the varieties layered so that none leads, with a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Open and generous within two or three years of the harvest, it gains breadth and a nutty depth over eight to ten years in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens in the glass; a white wine glass of good size.

label.means: Vienna's appellation since the 2013 vintage: at least three white varieties from one vineyard, picked and fermented together.

records.table: Wieninger's Ried Ulm is Vienna's field blend from one steep Nussberg slope above the Danube: nine white varieties picked and fermented together, with pear, quince and white pepper over a salty edge. Pour it cool beside roast chicken or a Heuriger plate.
records.story: Weingut Wieninger is a family estate of Stammersdorf, on the Bisamberg side of the Danube in the city's 21st district, with its own Heuriger, and its vineyards reach across the river onto the Nussberg above Nussdorf. Gemischter Satz, many white varieties planted together in one vineyard, had long been the everyday wine of the Heurigen, but its standing had slipped: beside wines of one variety it was taken for a blend of leftovers. The estate set out to show that the old field blend could make a serious wine. In 2006 four Viennese growers, Wieninger, Christ, Edlmoser and Zahel, founded the group WienWein to argue for the city's wine and its blend. The case was won with the 2013 vintage, when Wiener Gemischter Satz became a DAC with rules of its own: at least three white varieties from one vineyard, none above half the blend and the third at least a tenth. The estate turned to biodynamic farming in 2008, certified from the 2011 harvest. Its field blend from the Nussberg carries the name of its parcel, Ried Ulm, and the Erste Lage mark of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter. For a sommelier it is the case for the field blend as a wine of place.

The making (three quarters steel, a quarter large old oak, about ten months on fine lees), the nine varieties and the site rest on the house's sheets for 2018 and 2022 read through search; biodynamic since 2008 and certified from 2011 on the same sheets and the importer.
WienWein of 2006 and its four founders rest on the Drinks Business and the wein.plus glossary, with the ministry's page on Gemischter Satz (four growers in 2006); the DAC rules on Austrian Wine.

wine.name: Riesling Nussberg Weisser Marmor
wine.sites: One old vineyard on the Nussberg above Heiligenstadt and Nussdorf, about fifty years old in 2016 by the house's account, on calcareous soil of 25 to 65 per cent lime mixed with loam, clay and sand.
wine.making: Fermented and matured in stainless steel tanks with no oak, by Falstaff's listings across several vintages, for about a year in one vintage of the 2020s, so that the wine shows its fruit and the lime of its slope; it is made dry.
wine.glass: White peach, lime zest and green apple over wet stone, taut and finely knit, with lively acidity and a salty, chalky finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and taut in its first two years, it fills out over five to ten years and keeps well beyond that in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a Riesling glass or a white wine glass of good size.

records.table: Mayer am Pfarrplatz is the Heiligenstadt house where Beethoven lodged in 1817, and its Riesling Weisser Marmor grows on the shell limestone of the Nussberg above it: white peach and lime, taut, dry and salty. Pour it cool with fish or a schnitzel.
records.story: The house on the Pfarrplatz in Heiligenstadt, a village at the foot of the Vienna Woods that lies in the city's 19th district, has pressed wine since 1683 by its own account. In 1817 Ludwig van Beethoven (1770 to 1827) took rooms in its semi detached house, from May until the end of June, as his letters to a friend show; which works he sketched there is told in more than one way, so any one of them is a story rather than a record. The Mayer family kept a Heuriger and an estate here until the middle of the 2000s, when its head, with no heir to follow, handed both to a new owner who had already bought the Rotes Haus estate on the Nussberg; the Mayer name stayed on the door. The house later joined WienWein, the growers' group that argued for the city's field blend, and Wiener Gemischter Satz became a DAC with the 2013 vintage; its Gemischter Satz from the Preussen and the Langteufel, two Erste Lagen of the Nussberg, sit beside the Riesling. Weisser Marmor is the Riesling the house is known for, made in steel to show the lime of the hill. For a sommelier it joins a glass of Vienna to the summer that Beethoven spent among its vineyards.

A doubt on the pick for the checker: the house's Erste Lage wines (the Gemischter Satz and the Riesling of the Ried Preussen, the Gemischter Satz of the Ried Langteufel, all 1ÖTW) are arguably its leading wines, but the house itself names Weisser Marmor as the Riesling it is famous for, so the pick stands.

Beethoven's stay of May to the end of June 1817 rests on the house and the Österreichische Mediathek; which symphony he worked on there (the Ninth, or the Eroica in another account) is disputed and left out.
The sale of 2006 rests on Falstaff and Vinous, both naming the buyer, a living man, who is not named; that the new owners modernised and replanted is on Vinous alone and is left out.

The making rests on Falstaff's listings (steel tank for several vintages, twelve months for 2021); no house sheet was found, and hand picking and lees are left out. The meaning of the name Weisser Marmor is not explained by any source read.
The house's stand in WienWein (joined in 2009 by one account) is told without the year; that a head of the Mayer family urged Wieninger to keep making Gemischter Satz is on one source and left out.

wine.name: Wiener Gemischter Satz Ried Reisenberg
wine.grapes: A field blend of nine white varieties by the house's sheet: Traminer, Gelber Muskateller, Zierfandler, Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Chardonnay, Welschriesling, Weissburgunder and Rotgipfler.
wine.sites: Ried Reisenberg, the south facing slope of the hill above Grinzing on which the estate stands, the hill also called the Cobenzl; limestone with a cover of shell limestone over flysch sandstone and marl, in calcareous brown earth, farmed organically.

wine.glass: Rose petal, nectarine and pink grapefruit from the aromatic Traminer and Muskateller, over pear and a chalky, salty line; fresh, dry and supple, with a clean finish.
wine.ageing: Fresh and open on release, it holds and gains depth for ten years and more by the house's reckoning.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

records.table: Weingut Cobenzl's Gemischter Satz Ried Reisenberg grows on the hill above Grinzing that a count gave his name and the City of Vienna bought in 1907: nine varieties grown together, with rose petal, nectarine and grapefruit over a chalky line. Pour it cool.
records.story: Wine was grown on the Latisberg above Grinzing as early as the thirteenth century, the estate recounts. When the Jesuits who held the hill were dissolved in 1773, it passed to Count Johann Philipp Cobenzl (1741 to 1810), a statesman and diplomat of the Habsburg court, and the hill, once the Reisenberg, and the estate have carried his name since. In 1907 the City of Vienna bought the whole property, then a farm of fields and cattle meant to supply the city with grain and fresh milk. Vines took the leading part only later: the estate dates the building up of its vineyard to 1988, when the city engaged a winemaker for the task. The estate later joined the private houses of WienWein, the growers' group of 2006 that argued for the city's field blend, and Wiener Gemischter Satz became a DAC with the 2013 vintage. Its vineyards reach from Grinzing to the Nussberg and across the Danube to the Bisamberg. The Ried Reisenberg is the field blend from the hill of the estate itself, farmed organically, with Traminer and Muskateller in the planting to lift its scent. To a sommelier it shows what a city has made of its own slopes, and why a guest in Vienna drinks wine grown a tram ride from the centre.

report: The house writes its name Weingut Cobenzl on its own site; the City of Vienna and Falstaff's later listings write Weingut Wien Cobenzl. The plan's Weingut Cobenzl stands.

The year the count took the hill differs: 1774 on the estate's page, 1773 in the city's press release of 2007, 1776 in the Austria-Forum, so the story says the 1770s. His dates, 1741 to 1810, are on Britannica, the Wienbibliothek and the Austria-Forum.
The purchase of 1907, under the mayor of the day, rests on the estate's page and the Wien Geschichte Wiki (with its price, left out); ownership is told as history.

A doubt on the pick for the checker: the house's Ried Steinberg Gemischter Satz carries the 1ÖTW mark (Falstaff, the ÖTW map lists the Steinberg of Grinzing) and the Reisenberg does not, though the house's own Lagen page lists the Reisenberg among its first sites; the Reisenberg is kept as the field blend of the estate's own hill.

The making rests on Falstaff's listings (steel for 2015 to 2017, six months in amphora for 2022); hand picking is not confirmed and is left out. The nine varieties and the soil are on the house's sheet for the 2025 vintage; vine age is left out.

The engagement of a winemaker in 1988 is the estate's own account; the winemaker, living, is not named. The estate's place in WienWein rests on two portals (Meininger and wein.plus); the year it joined (2009 by one account) is left out.

wine.name: Wiener Gemischter Satz Ried Wiesthalen
wine.classification: Erste Lage of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter, marked 1ÖTW on the label
wine.grapes: A field blend of several white varieties planted together in one old vineyard, as the DAC requires; the house does not list them.
wine.sites: Ried Wiesthalen, an old site of the Bisamberg by the house's account, on its south east slope above Jedlersdorf on the Danube's left bank; flysch sandstone, coral limestone and clay, farmed organically.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented together with wild yeasts in French oak barrels, as a Gemischter Satz must be made together. It then rests on its lees in barrel for more than a year, thirteen months on one of the house's pages and about eighteen on its sheet for the 2024 vintage, and is bottled without fining or sterile filtration.
wine.glass: Ripe yellow peach, juicy apple and brioche over a salty, chalky line; full and textured from its long time in wood, yet dry and fresh to the finish.
wine.ageing: Open on release after its long time in barrel, it has the build to keep and deepen for several years more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly if it seems closed; a white wine glass of good size.

records.table: Weingut Christ's Gemischter Satz Ried Wiesthalen is the left bank's field blend: a Bisamberg slope above Jedlersdorf, picked by hand, fermented together and long in barrel, with yellow peach, apple and brioche. Pour it with roast pork at the Heuriger.
records.story: The Christ family has farmed at Jedlersdorf, north of the Danube in the city's 21st district, for about four hundred years by its own account, beginning with a small mixed farm in a village that then stood on an island in the river's wetlands. Its Heuriger began in 1927, the house tells, with two tables in the family's own kitchen, and moved into a room of its own in 1959. In the 1980s the family gave up cattle and field crops to grow vines alone. In 2006 Christ was one of the four growers who founded WienWein to argue for the city's wine and its field blend, and Wiener Gemischter Satz became a DAC with the 2013 vintage. The whole estate has been farmed organically since 2014, when the Petershof, an organic holding, joined it. The Ried Wiesthalen, on the south east slope of the Bisamberg, carries the Erste Lage mark of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter, and its field blend, picked by hand and long in barrel, shows a weightier side of Vienna's wine than the young Gemischter Satz of the taverns. For a sommelier it is the left bank's answer to the Nussberg across the river.

The house's claim that the Petershof was the oldest certified organic vineyard of Vienna is left out; the Heurigen culture's national listing by UNESCO in 2019, on the house's timeline, is left out.

wine.name: Wiener Gemischter Satz Ried Kaasgraben
wine.grapes: A field blend of white varieties grown together, among them Chardonnay, Riesling, Grüner Veltliner, Rotgipfler, Zierfandler and Neuburger, by the house's sheet.
wine.sites: Ried Kaasgraben, a small north east facing plot in the 19th district that the house lists under the Nussberg, below the Kaasgrabenkirche; sandy loam over flysch sandstone and weathered shell limestone.
wine.making: Picked by hand, the grapes rest on their skins in the press for about a day and a half before pressing. The must ferments with its own yeasts in large Austrian oak casks from the cooper Stockinger and rests about eighteen months on its fine lees; the vines are farmed biodynamically, Demeter certified.
wine.glass: Ripe pear, quince and lemon peel with a waft of honey over a salty, chalky line; textured from its time on the skins and in large wood, dry and long.
wine.ageing: Open on release, it has the grip and texture to keep and gain depth for several years more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant briefly if it seems closed; a white wine glass of good size.

records.table: Zahel is a Mauer family house, and its Gemischter Satz Ried Kaasgraben is a field blend from a small slope by the Nussberg: a day and a half on the skins, wild yeasts and large Austrian casks give pear, quince and a chalky grip. Serve it cool.
records.story: Mauer, at the city's southern edge, is the southernmost of Vienna's old vine villages, and the Zahel family keeps its Heuriger on the main square there. The great grandparents of the present generation first opened the tavern in 1930, the house recounts, with the bar room as its only room. In 1966, by the house's account, a member of the family selected the Orangetraube, a white variety long grown in the family's mixed plantings, and planted a vineyard of it alone. In 1989 a new generation took the estate over. In 2006 Zahel was one of the four growers who founded WienWein, a group that argued for the city's field blend, and Wiener Gemischter Satz became a DAC with the 2013 vintage. The estate went organic from the 2017 vintage and was certified by Demeter from 2018. Its vineyards run from the Maurerberg in the south to the Nussberg in the north, and the Ried Kaasgraben, made with skin contact and in large wood, is its field blend from the north. For a sommelier it shows that a Gemischter Satz need not be light.

report: The Kaasgraben lies in the 19th district, listed by the house under the Grosslage Nussberg, not in Mauer: the plan's note asked where it lies, and the house and its importer agree. That it leads the range is not stated by any source read; the house's Ried Mauerberg and its Orangetraube are as prominent, and the checker may weigh them.
The cask size differs: 1,200 litres on the house's sheet, 600 litres on an importer's, so the record says large casks. The skin contact of 36 hours and the wild ferment are the house's sheet.

Founded is left empty: the house dates its Heuriger to 1930, with the importer, but gives no founding of the estate; the bar room's building as a school of Maria Theresa about four hundred years ago is the house's claim and is left out.

The region record's old mixed plantings on the Maurer Berg are confirmed only in general (old vines of the Kroissberg and the Maurerberg on importers' sheets), so the record speaks of mixed plantings and the Orangetraube of 1966 alone. The member of the family who planted it in 1966 is described, not named, his dates not found.

The claim that Zahel is the only Austrian house to bottle Orangetraube alone and its regenerative organic certificate of 2024 are left out. Organic from 2017 and Demeter from 2018 rest on the house and its importer.
Living members of the family are not named. Searches for this house: 4.
